Adjudicating between those two readings starts with the institutional record behind the transition itself. Chief Michel Moor's April 2020 memo attributed PredPol's shutdown specifically to the city's COVID-19 financial crisis and mayoral belt-tightening, not to the racial-bias scrutiny activists and journalists were raising at the same time [@cushing_2020_lapds-failed-predictive-policing]. That the same chief who discontinued PredPol said he still believed in location-based strategies going forward [@cushing_2020_lapds-failed-predictive-policing] is worth noting before taking DICFP's stated break from PredPol's logic at face value.

Critics argue DICFP borrows its targeting logic from Operation LASER, LAPD's earlier person-based program, and continues to direct enforcement toward areas with already-high call volume [@wille_2021_lapds-new-data-driven-policing; @stop-lapd-spying-coalition_2021_automating-banishment]. In other words, they allege that the LAPD automates the same underlying logic rather than reforming it . That claim has been made qualitatively but not tested against tract-level enforcement data.

This is verified directly against LAPD's own April 2020 guidebook: the data feeding hotspot targeting is unchanged from the PredPol/LASER era. Calls for Service, crime/incident reports, and Palantir/CAMS-based kernel density estimation on 500-1,000 foot "micro-geographic locations" [@los-angeles-police-department_2020_data-informed-community-focused, pp. 10-13, 22], functionally the same approach as PredPol's 500x500 sq ft grid cells. The guidebook does introduce community surveys, but they measure trust, fear, and satisfaction with police services (an "Assessment"/outcome metric [@los-angeles-police-department_2020_data-informed-community-focused, Ch. 6, pp. 25-27]). None of these data report victimization independent of police contact. Nothing in the document describes survey results (e.g., detected underreporting or distrust in a given neighborhood) feeding back into what counts as a hotspot or where enforcement gets targeted; that pipeline [@los-angeles-police-department_2020_data-informed-community-focused, Ch. 3] draws only on CFS/crime-report volume. Absence of a described feedback mechanism in a public guidebook is not proof that no such mechanism exists internally, so this should be read as an evidentiary gap rather than a settled fact.

The two readings raised at the outset cash out as directly testable predictions. If DICFP is genuine reform, spatial concentration should shift relative to the PredPol era; if it is a cosmetic rebrand of PredPol/LASER's targeting logic, spatial concentration should persist unchanged despite the stated goals. The literature reviewed next situates that test within the broader predictive-policing scholarship before turning to how it is operationalized.
